# IronGall v1 test vectors

Files any IronGall implementation can check itself against, made with stock tools (`generate.sh`: bash, od, base64, sha256sum, ssh-keygen, and age ≥ 1.3 for the two ciphertexts), and the few that no stock tool can write by a Go test, from the same published keys (`IRONGALL_WRITE_VECTORS=1 go test ./protocol`, `protocol/vectors_test.go`). Every vector is judged at the time in `now`.

**The keys are public test keys.** The Ed25519 ones are RFC 8032's (`input/*.ed25519`: the seed, then the public key, in hex): from §7.1, box A's identity is TEST 1 and box B's is TEST 2, A's working key is TEST 3, B's is TEST 1024, and a second working key of A's is TEST SHA(abc); from §7.2, box C's working key is the first Ed25519ctx test's key. Box C's identity is of the optional type `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`: the test key of RFC 6979 §A.2.5 (`input/c.p256`: the private scalar, then the public point as x and y, in hex). B's and C's prekeys are the published test identities of C2SP's age testkit (CCTV `age/internal/testkit`): `input/b-1.pq.key` is its `TestHybridIdentity` and `input/c-1.classic.key` its `TestX25519Identity`, so each message here decrypts with any age implementation. The other age recipients in `input/` are public keys whose secret keys were discarded.

| Path | What | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `a/`, `b/` | each box's `identity.doc` and `address`; `work-cert.pub`, its identity's certificate for its working key; its prekey statements `prekey-<serial>.txt` with `.sig`, signed by the working key; A's `revoke.txt` with `revoke.sig`, its revocation, signed by the identity itself, and `revoke.sha256.sig`, the same with SHA-256, which verifiers accept; and A's `pass.txt`, `pass.sig` and `pass.authorization`, a pass for a server it calls `irongall.example` | all valid. `a/prekey-1` is post-quantum, `a/prekey-2` X25519 only (`--no-pq`); `a/prekey-1.txt.sha256.sig` signs with SHA-256 instead of SHA-512, which verifiers accept. The pass runs out ten minutes after `now` |
| `c/` | box C, whose identity is a P-256 key: its `identity.doc` (173 bytes) and `address`, `work-cert.pub`, `prekey-1.txt` with `.sig`, and `revoke.txt` with `revoke.sig`, its revocation, made once and kept | valid for a client that verifies `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`. One that does not refuses the document with its code for a key type it lacks, never as malformed |
| `cert/bad-*` | a certificate (`.pub`) that breaks one rule, and a signature made under it (`.sig`) over `a/prekey-1.txt` in A's prekey namespace | every one refused for box A. The signature is good under the certificate it carries: the certificate is what fails. `bad-serial-above-2-53` is numbered 2^53, one above the highest serial. `bad-extension-twice` gives an extension's name twice, and `bad-extension-value-an-empty-string` an extension's value as one empty string: neither is the one encoding Go's `x/crypto/ssh` reads, each name once, in lexical order, and a value nothing or one string that is not empty. `ssh-keygen -Y verify` alone takes those two, `bad-key-id` and `bad-serial-zero` |
| `revoke/bad-*.sig` | a signature that is not a revocation of box A: `bad-by-a-working-key` (A's working key over A's statement, under A's own certificate), `bad-by-another-identity` (B's identity over A's statement), `bad-another-namespace` (A's identity over A's statement, in the prekey namespace), `bad-of-another-box` (A's identity over B's statement), `bad-s-plus-l` (A's own revocation, with L added to its S) | every one refused as a revocation of A. `ssh-keygen -Y verify` takes `bad-by-a-working-key` when the identity is named a `cert-authority`, so a verifier's signers line for a revocation never says so |
| `revoked/ok-*` | a revocation of box A's certificates (`.txt`) and A's identity's signature over it (`.sig`): `ok-through-4` (every certificate up to and including serial 4, with `.sha256.sig` in the other hash) and `ok-through-the-highest` (through 2^53 − 1, the highest serial there is) | taken as revocations of A's certificates, each through exactly that serial |
| `revoked/bad-*` | what is not a revocation of A's certificates, each with a signature that is good over its bytes: `bad-by-a-working-key` (A's working key, under A's own certificate), `bad-another-namespace` (A's identity, in the revocation's namespace), `bad-another-address` (B's address in it), and one for each rule of the text (no serial; a serial of zero, with a leading zero, a sign or a trailing space, of 19 digits or above 2^53 − 1; a range; a second serial; a blank line; CRLF; no final newline; another tag; the address in uppercase; a NUL; and `bad-a-list`, the list a certificate was revoked by until 2026-10-14); and `bad-s-plus-l`, a good one whose signature has L added to its S | every one refused. `ssh-keygen -Y verify` takes each of the malformed ones, since the signature is good: the text is what fails, and a shell reader that tests a variable alone takes `bad-nul`. It takes `bad-s-plus-l` too, on an OpenSSH built on its own Ed25519, as it takes `revoke/bad-s-plus-l` |
| `sig/ok-*`, `sig/bad-*` | `a/prekey-1.txt.sig` in other forms, each over `a/prekey-1.txt` in A's prekey namespace, under A's certificate (PROTOCOL.md §3). `ok-*`: CRLF line ends, CRLF after the BEGIN line only, a space and a tab in the base64, a VT and an FF there, a blank line before the END line, the base64 on one line, no line feed after the END line, text after it, the file padded after it to exactly 4096 bytes, and a blob whose `reserved` field holds bytes the key did not sign. `bad-*`: 4097 bytes, after the END line or as spaces before it; a space after the BEGIN line, text before it, no END line, an END line indented; a character outside base64, a NUL, a padding bit set, the padding gone; a byte after the blob's five fields; and an Ed25519 S with L added, the working key's (`bad-s-plus-l`) or the identity's on the certificate (`bad-certificate-s-plus-l`) | `ok-*` taken, `bad-*` refused, as `ssh-keygen -Y verify` judges each but four: it takes both of 4097 bytes, and on an OpenSSH built on its own Ed25519 (10.2p1, Ubuntu) both S + L. Those a verifier refuses by its own checks |
| `cert/ok-*` | a certificate at the edge of a rule, and a signature made under it, as `cert/bad-*` | taken. `ok-begins-now` begins at `now`; `bad-not-begun` begins a second later. `ok-extensions` carries the five extensions `ssh-keygen` adds without `-O clear`, and `ok-unknown-extension` one nobody defines, with a value: a verifier knows none, and ignores each. `ok-reserved-field` holds bytes in its reserved field, which a verifier ignores too; `ssh-keygen` writes that field empty, so `protocol`'s `TestVectorsReservedField` makes it |
| `message/` | `a-to-b.line`, an envelope from A to B as its one line; `a-to-b.sig`, A's working key's signature over it for B; `a-to-b.plain`, what is encrypted (the line, the signature, the padding); `a-to-b.age`, that encrypted to B's post-quantum prekey. `a-to-c.*`, the same to C's X25519 prekey | the line and the signature are what a client makes from the same keys, byte for byte; each age file is a whole number of blocks and decrypts with its prekey's published identity to exactly its `.plain` |
| `plain/accept-*`, `refuse-*` | what box B decrypts | delivered or refused, as named, with these codes: `refuse-no-line-feed`, `-no-signature`, `-blank-line-before-the-signature`, `-signature-first`, `-no-end-line`, `-end-line-without-its-line-feed`, `-crlf` and `-envelope-on-two-lines` as `bad_message`; `refuse-signature-over-4096-bytes` (spaces in its base64) as `bad_signature`; `refuse-end-line-followed-by-a-nul` and `refuse-end-line-followed-by-a-byte-and-a-later-one` (a byte after the END line, then an END line and its line feed in the padding: the block ends at the first) as `bad_message`; `refuse-begin-line-followed-by-a-nul`, `-holding-a-nul` and `-preceded-by-a-nul` as `bad_message`, since there is no BEGIN line; `refuse-no-identity`, `-identity-not-base64`, `-identity-of-small-order`, `-identity-off-curve`, `-identity-ending-in-a-line-feed` and `-identity-ending-in-a-nul` (each a JSON escape) as `bad_identity`; `refuse-signed-for-another-box`, `-signed-by-the-identity`, `-signed-by-a-bare-working-key`, `-certificate-ended`, `-line-changed-after-signing` and `-another-box-s-identity-document` as `bad_signature`; `refuse-from-is-not-the-identity`, `-from-is-not-the-identity-of-an-unknown-type`, `-from-null` (null is a member left out) and `-to-another-box` as `reattributed`; `refuse-unsupported-key-type` as `unsupported_key_type`. `accept-p256-sender` is from box C: delivered by a client that verifies `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, and `unsupported_key_type` to one that does not. `accept-whitespace-in-the-signature` has a space, a CR and a tab in its base64, which every verifier skips. In `accept-anything-after-the-signature` a second envelope, signed by B, follows the first END line and is never read. `refuse-another-box-s-identity-document` is the forgery an identity member invites: A's document beside a certificate B's identity signed |
| `identity/*.doc` | malformed identity documents, and well-formed ones holding a key that fails its type's checks: an Ed25519 key that is of small order, not canonical, or (`off-curve`) no point on the curve, or (`p256-*`) a P-256 point that is off the curve, compressed, not reduced or the point at infinity (`p256-point-at-infinity`, one zero byte, as SEC1 writes it). `ok-p256-short-coordinate` (x = 5) and `ok-p256-coordinate-over-order` (x = n + 3) are points on the curve that OpenSSH refused up to 10.2p1, and takes from 10.3p1, as Go's library does and the protocol does (PROTOCOL.md §2). `type-name-ending-in-nul` and `p256-curve-name-ending-in-nul` are A's and C's keys with a NUL ending the type's or the curve's name: `ssh-keygen` reads each as that box's key and writes it back without the NUL, so neither is the key in its one encoding. `unsupported-type.doc` is a well-formed document of a key type nobody verifies. `nul-*` and `p256-nul-*` hold a NUL byte, in place of a line feed or elsewhere, and are as long as a good document | `ok-*` taken by a client that verifies `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, as `c/identity.doc` is; every other one rejected: `unsupported-type.doc` as a key type the client does not verify, the rest as a bad document or a bad key |
| `prekey/bad-*` | prekey statements with a `.sig` by A's working key, in A's namespace, except where the name says otherwise | every one rejected, `bad-serial-above-2-53` among them: a serial is at most 2^53 − 1, since an answer names one as a JSON number. `bad-outlives-its-certificate` is signed under the certificate beside it, which ends in ten days. `bad-nul-in-*` each hold a NUL in one line, which a reader that takes the line through a shell variable drops, and `bad-serial-a-digit-not-ascii` a serial with U+0661, which `[0-9]` takes in some locales |
| `prekey/expired` | a valid statement whose `not_after` is `now` | valid, but expired: a sender must not encrypt to it |
| `prekey/longest` | a valid statement that ends 33 days and an hour after `now` | not expired, and the longest a server takes: an hour past what a client asks for |
| `prekey/too-long` | a valid statement that ends a second later than that | not expired, but a server must refuse to publish it |
| `prekey/unsupported-type` | a statement good in every way but its key: a well-formed age recipient of a type nobody defines, RFC 7748 §6.1's published X25519 test key (Alice's public key) under the human-readable part `age1nosuchtype` | refused with its own code, `unsupported_prekey_type`, never as a statement that does not verify: a sender cannot encrypt to it, and nothing is wrong with it (PROTOCOL.md §0a) |
| `envelope/accept-*`, `refuse-*` | envelopes of a message whose signature by A verified, received by B | accepted or refused, as named. Keys match exactly and none may appear twice, so every reader takes the same values: in `accept-case-variant-key` the body is `"benign"` (`BODY` is an unknown key, ignored); `refuse-duplicate-key` has two `from`s; `refuse-version-string` has `"v":"1"`, which is not the number 1; `refuse-not-utf8` and `refuse-two-objects` are not one UTF-8 JSON object. Strict on what a loose reader lets through: `refuse-msg-id-newline` ends its `msg_id` with a newline, `refuse-msg-id-grouped-wrongly` has 36 characters and four hyphens, out of RFC 9562's places, `refuse-subject-number` has a number where a string goes, and `refuse-sent-at-second-60` names a second some date parsers carry into the next minute. The envelope is a JSON text as PROTOCOL.md §0b reads one, its body included: `accept-body-nested-to-32` is taken, and `refuse-body-nested-to-33`, `-key-twice-in-the-body`, `-nan-in-the-body`, `-leading-zero-in-the-body`, `-noncharacter-in-the-body`, `-above-u10ffff-in-the-body` and `-byte-order-mark` are refused. The window of `sent_at` has a vector on each side of each end: `accept-33-days-old` and `refuse-33-days-and-1s-old` (refused as `stale`), `accept-1-hour-ahead` and `refuse-1-hour-and-1s-ahead` (refused as `future`). `v` is an integer member, written in digits alone: `refuse-version-written-with-a-fraction` (`1.0`), `-written-with-an-exponent` (`1e0`), `-a-decimal-just-above-1` and `-nul-after-the-version` (a raw NUL, which jq drops). `refuse-sent-at-ending-in-a-line-feed` and `-ending-in-a-nul` are JSON escapes a shell variable would drop. Every refusal is `bad_envelope` to the Go client but `stale`, `future`, and `reattributed` for `refuse-from-not-signer`, `-from-null` and `-to-another-box`; an uppercase `from` or `to` (`refuse-from-uppercase`, `-to-uppercase`) is no address, so `bad_envelope`. The stock script is held to every `accept-*` and to the refusals that guard a forgery or a replay (`envelopeFive` in `sh/sh_test.go`, `stale` and `future` by name); the rest are the Go client's (`AGENTS.md` § The shell client) |
| `json/ok-*`, `json/bad-*` | JSON texts, each breaking one rule of PROTOCOL.md §0b or none: a byte-order mark; bytes that are not UTF-8, an overlong form, a surrogate, a code point above U+10FFFF, a five-byte form; a lone surrogate escaped, high, low and low in a name (jq reads a lone low one as U+FFFD); a noncharacter written, escaped, in plane 16 and in a name; a control character, a unit separator (jq 1.7.0 takes it) and a NUL after a number (jq ends the number there and drops it); a name twice, in a nested object and through an escape; a second value, a bracket or a brace after the object; an array, a string, nothing; `NaN`, `nan`, `-Infinity`, `01`, `+1`, `.5`, `1.`; a trailing comma, single quotes, a vertical tab; and nesting to 33. `ok-*` hold what is allowed: whitespace, any JSON number, every escape, a surrogate pair, the code points beside the noncharacters, one name in two objects, and nesting to 32 | `ok-*` taken and `bad-*` refused, by every reader the protocol defines, whatever kind of text it expects; the stock script is not held to these (`AGENTS.md` § The shell client) |
| `answer/<kind>-ok-*`, `answer/<kind>-bad-*` | whole answers of a server, of each kind a client reads as JSON: `box` (the read of a box), `list`, `record` (a revocation record), `receipt` and `problem` (an error). A fetch answers a message's ciphertext alone, which is no JSON, so it has none. The bad ones: a byte member that is a number, unpadded, wrapped or with its unused bits set; a member twice, null after a value, `NaN` beside the record, a second value, nothing, an array; an integer member that is negative, above 2^53 − 1, a fraction or written with one, or written with an exponent (`list-bad-count-written-with-an-exponent`); a string or an object where another type goes (`list-bad-from-a-number`: who sent a message is its list entry's); a list's cursor that is not one or more of `A`–`Z`, `a`–`z`, `0`–`9`, `-` and `_` (`list-bad-cursor-a-slash`, `-a-percent`, `-empty`), where `list-ok-cursor` holds the whole alphabet; a problem whose `code` comes before a member that breaks it, which carries no code. The ok ones: null members, unknown members, names in another case (which are unknown members: such a record shows nothing), and `{}` | `<kind>-ok-*` taken and `<kind>-bad-*` no answer, as the Go client reads that kind (the stock script takes every `ok` one and refuses the `bad` ones whose broken member it reads, `answerRead` in `sh/sh_test.go`): a `2xx` revocations answer that is no record stops a drain with the mail still on the server |
| `pass/ok-*`, `pass/bad-*` | `a/pass.authorization` in other forms, each an `Authorization` value with no line feed after it: the scheme and the names in other cases, another order, whitespace around commas and `=`, the address as a token, empty list elements; then what is no pass, a tab after the scheme, a parameter twice or unknown or missing, a backslash in a quoted value, `not_after` as a token, a space in the signature, an address in capitals and others. `ok-as-a-sender-writes-it` is the one form a client writes (PROTOCOL.md §6.1b) | `ok-*`: read as the same three values as `a/pass.authorization`, so each verifies for box A at `./now` as that pass does. `bad-*`: no pass, `401 unauthorized` at a server |

Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so an implementation that signs these statements with these keys, under these certificates, must produce byte-identical `.sig` files. A certificate is made once and kept, since `ssh-keygen` puts a random nonce in one, and so is each `message/*.age`, since age encryption is randomised; everything else regenerates byte for byte.

**The crypto and container vectors are checked by tools this project did not write** (`protocol`'s `TestVectorsByToolsNotOurs`, which skips a tool that is missing and says so): `age` decrypts each `message/*.age` with its prekey's published identity to exactly its `.plain` (the age on `PATH` when it reads post-quantum files, else the one `go.mod` names as a tool, which is the version the client links); `head -n 1` and `sed -n '2,/^-----END SSH SIGNATURE-----$/p'` split each plaintext into its `.line` and `.sig`; `ssh-keygen -L` reads every certificate, and `ssh-keygen -Y verify`, at `now`, verifies every signature in `a/`, `b/`, `c/` and `message/`, each `cert/ok-*` under its certificate and each `revoked/ok-*`, a working key's under its identity as `cert-authority` and an identity's own under its bare key; `sha256sum` gives each address from its identity document. So each of those is the standard's format, not this code's reading of it. **A second age implementation read both ciphertexts once,** since `age` above is filippo.io/age, the library this client encrypts with: typage (`age-encryption` 0.3.1 on npm, with `@noble/post-quantum` 0.5.4, `@noble/curves` 2.0.1, `@noble/hashes` 2.0.1, `@noble/ciphers` 2.4.0 and `@scure/base` 2.4.0, each tarball checked against the registry's integrity hash) decrypted `message/a-to-b.age` (sha256 `ad48a5242950208f9052ce40bba8b7b88eee649d9f600647ba3c555b098c2f64`) and `message/a-to-c.age` (sha256 `1e15570d99cd5cbc20c467f3d389dcb06344e1d388bd07e611aa450d319be4ee`) to exactly their `.plain` on 2026-10-21, and derived each prekey's recipient from its identity; with one byte flipped it refused the file. `generate.sh` keeps both files, so that holds while their hashes match: a file made again is read by a second implementation again. Every other vector is this project's own conformance check: an implementation gives it its named verdict.
